questions.stem: The Ptolemaic dynasty that Cleopatra VII belonged to was founded by Ptolemy I, who was:
options: a native Egyptian high priest of Amun at Thebes
a Roman governor appointed by the senate
a Persian satrap left in charge of Egypt
a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great
questions.explanation: After Alexander died in 323 BCE, his general Ptolemy took control of Egypt and founded a Greek-speaking Macedonian dynasty that ruled from Alexandria for nearly three centuries. Egypt did not become Roman until Cleopatra's death in 30 BCE.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the nature of royal power in Ptolemaic Egypt?
options: The ruler governed as a Roman client and needed the senate to approve every new law
The ruler was a Greek-speaking monarch at Alexandria who also acted as pharaoh to Egyptians
The ruler was elected for life by an assembly of the Greek and Egyptian citizens of Alexandria
The ruler shared equal power with a council of priests who could veto any royal decree
questions.explanation: The Ptolemies ran a Greek court and administration from Alexandria, yet presented themselves in temples and inscriptions as traditional pharaohs honouring the Egyptian gods. Rome's influence grew in the first century BCE, but the senate did not approve Egyptian laws.

questions.stem: In 55 BCE Cleopatra's father, Ptolemy XII, was restored to his throne by Aulus Gabinius, the Roman governor of Syria, after being driven out of Alexandria. This shows that in Cleopatra's youth:
options: the Ptolemies had stopped making alliances with foreign powers
holding the Egyptian throne increasingly depended on Roman support
Egypt had already been annexed as a province of the Roman Republic
the Egyptian army was strong enough to defeat any Roman invasion
questions.explanation: Ptolemy XII had paid heavily for Roman recognition, and when he was expelled it was a Roman army that put him back. Cleopatra learned early that Ptolemaic power rested on winning powerful Romans, though Egypt stayed independent until 30 BCE.

questions.stem: According to Plutarch, Cleopatra differed from the Ptolemaic kings before her because she:
options: refused to allow Greek to be spoken at her court
was born and raised in Rome
never married any of her brothers
learned the native Egyptian language
questions.explanation: Plutarch says the earlier kings of Egypt had not even tried to learn the native language, while Cleopatra spoke it along with many others. Her first language was Greek, the language of the Ptolemaic court.

questions.stem: Cleopatra's mother is not securely identified in the ancient evidence. What is the most defensible conclusion a historian can draw from this?
options: The gap proves the ancient writers deliberately invented her family
Her ancestry on her mother's side cannot be known with certainty
Her mother must have been a Roman noblewoman from Caesar's family
Her mother must have been her father's sister, as Ptolemaic custom required
questions.explanation: Because the sources do not settle who her mother was, confident claims about her maternal ancestry go beyond the evidence. A gap in the record is a limit on knowledge, not proof of invention or of any one answer.

questions.stem: When Ptolemy XII died in 51 BCE, his will left the throne to:
options: Cleopatra jointly with her younger brother Ptolemy XIII
Cleopatra alone, with Pompey as her co-regent
her older sister Berenice IV and her husband
her younger sister Arsinoe IV jointly with Ptolemy XIV
questions.explanation: Cleopatra, then about eighteen, became joint ruler with her brother Ptolemy XIII, following the Ptolemaic custom of sibling co-rule. Berenice IV had seized the throne during their father's exile and was executed when he returned.

questions.stem: A stele records the installation of a sacred Buchis bull at Hermonthis, near Thebes, in 51 BCE, early in Cleopatra's reign. It is useful evidence that Cleopatra:
options: relied on Roman troops to keep order in the temples of Upper Egypt
was dominated by her brother's advisers during the first years of her reign
presented herself to Egyptians as a traditional pharaoh honouring the gods
rejected Egyptian religion in favour of the gods of the Greek city of Alexandria
questions.explanation: Supporting an Egyptian bull cult was a pharaonic duty, so the stele shows the image of a pious Egyptian ruler that Cleopatra wished to project. Official inscriptions show how a ruler wanted to be seen, so they are less reliable for her private beliefs.

questions.stem: By 48 BCE Cleopatra had been driven out of Alexandria by her brother's advisers. Her response was to:
options: raise an army in Syria and march back to the Egyptian border
flee to Rome and ask the senate to declare war on Egypt
accept exile in Cyprus and give up her claim to the throne
marry Pompey and use his surviving legions to retake Alexandria
questions.explanation: Cleopatra gathered forces in Syria and camped near Pelusium on Egypt's eastern frontier, facing her brother's army. It was during this stand-off that Pompey arrived in Egypt after Pharsalus and was killed by agents of Ptolemy XIII's court.

questions.stem: Popular retellings say Cleopatra was carried to Caesar rolled up in a carpet. Plutarch, the main ancient source for the meeting, says she was:
options: brought by Roman soldiers after her capture at Pelusium
rowed into the royal harbour on a gilded barge dressed as Venus
tied inside a bed-sack carried in by Apollodorus the Sicilian
dressed as a servant and led through the gates by Pothinus
questions.explanation: In Plutarch's Life of Caesar, Apollodorus tied her into a bed-sack and carried it indoors to Caesar. The carpet is a later embellishment, and the gilded barge belongs to Plutarch's account of her meeting with Antony at Tarsus in 41 BCE.

questions.stem: Which outcome of the Alexandrian War of 48-47 BCE strengthened Cleopatra's position most?
options: Caesar made her son Caesarion the heir to his estate
Pothinus and Achillas swore loyalty to her as the sole ruler of Egypt
Ptolemy XIII drowned and Arsinoe IV was captured by Caesar
The Roman senate crowned her queen of Egypt in Rome
questions.explanation: Her brother drowned in the Nile while fleeing, and her sister Arsinoe, who had claimed the throne, was captured and later paraded in Caesar's triumph in Rome. Cleopatra was restored with her younger brother Ptolemy XIV as a nominal co-ruler.

questions.stem: Cleopatra's son Caesarion, born in 47 BCE, was officially known as:
options: Ptolemy XIV Philopator
Alexander Helios
Ptolemy Philadelphus
Ptolemy XV Caesar
questions.explanation: Caesarion ('little Caesar') was the name used by others; as king he was Ptolemy XV Caesar, his mother's co-ruler from 44 BCE. Ptolemy XIV was her brother, and Alexander Helios and Ptolemy Philadelphus were her sons by Antony.

questions.stem: Cleopatra was in Rome from 46 to 44 BCE, and Caesar placed a gilded statue of her in his new Temple of Venus Genetrix. Why did this alarm many Romans?
options: It proved that Caesar planned to move the capital of the empire to Egypt
It linked a foreign queen with the goddess Caesar claimed as his ancestor
It showed that Caesar had formally married her under Roman law that year
It meant Cleopatra had been granted a seat and a vote in the Roman senate
questions.explanation: Venus Genetrix was honoured as the mother of the Julian family, so a statue of the queen in her temple suggested Caesar was drawing close to Hellenistic monarchy. Roman law did not allow a marriage between a citizen and a foreign queen, and Caesar's wife remained Calpurnia.

questions.stem: In a letter to Atticus written after Caesar's death, Cicero wrote 'reginam odi' ('I hate the queen') and complained of her arrogance while she was staying across the Tiber. As evidence about Cleopatra, the letter is:
options: an Egyptian source that reflects the views of her own court
a contemporary account by someone who met her, but personally hostile
a neutral record written for the public archives of the senate
a later invention by Augustan writers that was falsely attributed to Cicero
questions.explanation: Cicero knew Cleopatra and wrote privately at the time, which makes the letter valuable. He was also offended by her and opposed to Caesar's circle, so it shows a Roman senator's hostility more than a balanced judgment.

questions.stem: After her brother Ptolemy XIV died in 44 BCE, Cleopatra made her co-ruler:
options: her sister Arsinoe IV
the triumvir Mark Antony
her son Alexander Helios
her son Caesarion
questions.explanation: From 44 BCE Cleopatra ruled with Caesarion as Ptolemy XV, securing the throne for her own line. Antony never held the Egyptian throne, and Alexander Helios was not born until 40 BCE.

questions.stem: Where did Cleopatra meet Mark Antony in 41 BCE, beginning their alliance?
options: Tarsus, in Cilicia
Rome, at Caesar's villa
Athens, in Greece
Actium, in western Greece
questions.explanation: Antony summoned Cleopatra to Tarsus to answer for her conduct in the civil war against Caesar's assassins. Plutarch describes her sailing up the river Cydnus in a gilded barge, adorned like Venus in a painting.

questions.stem: Why was an alliance with Mark Antony so valuable to Cleopatra after 42 BCE?
options: He was sole ruler of Rome and could make Caesarion heir to the whole empire
He had promised to make Egypt a Roman province with Cleopatra as its first governor
He commanded the only Roman fleet in the Mediterranean after Pompey's death
He controlled Rome's eastern provinces and could protect and enlarge her kingdom
questions.explanation: After Philippi the triumvirs divided responsibilities and Antony took charge of the East, where Egypt lay. He needed Egyptian money and supplies for his planned Parthian campaign, while she needed Roman backing and territory.

questions.stem: Cleopatra's children with Mark Antony were:
options: Alexander Helios, Caesarion and Cleopatra Selene
Cleopatra Selene, Ptolemy Philadelphus and Caesarion
Alexander Helios, Cleopatra Selene and Ptolemy Philadelphus
Caesarion, Arsinoe IV and Ptolemy XIV
questions.explanation: The twins Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene were born in 40 BCE and Ptolemy Philadelphus in 36 BCE. Caesarion was Caesar's son, and Arsinoe IV, Ptolemy XIII and Ptolemy XIV were Cleopatra's siblings.

questions.stem: In 40 BCE Antony married Octavia, the sister of Octavian, and did not see Cleopatra again until 37 BCE. This suggests that at that time:
options: Antony's alliance with Octavian mattered more to him than Cleopatra
Cleopatra had broken off the alliance to rule in partnership with the Parthians
Roman law forced every triumvir to marry a senator's daughter
Octavia had been chosen by Cleopatra to keep the peace with Rome
questions.explanation: The marriage sealed the agreement at Brundisium between the triumvirs, showing that Roman politics came first for Antony. It also warns against reading the relationship only as a romance, as later writers often did.

questions.stem: From 37-36 BCE Antony granted Cleopatra territories including Cyprus and parts of Phoenicia, Coele-Syria and Cilicia. Her most likely aim in seeking these lands was to:
options: move her capital out of Alexandria to escape Roman influence
give the lands to her brother Ptolemy XIV as his own kingdom
restore the Ptolemaic empire and gain timber, revenue and coastline
found Roman colonies for Antony's veterans along the eastern Mediterranean coast
questions.explanation: Earlier Ptolemies had ruled these regions, and they offered shipbuilding timber and income. Ptolemy XIV had died in 44 BCE, so he could not be the beneficiary.

questions.stem: According to Plutarch, at the Donations of Alexandria in 34 BCE Antony:
options: gave Judaea to Ptolemy Philadelphus as a gift
allotted Armenia, Media and Parthia to Alexander Helios
handed all of Rome's western provinces over to Caesarion
made Cleopatra Selene queen of Italy and Sicily
questions.explanation: Plutarch says Antony declared Cleopatra queen of Egypt, Cyprus, Libya and Coele-Syria, sharing her throne with Caesarion, and named his sons Kings of Kings, giving Alexander Armenia, Media and Parthia and Ptolemy Phoenicia, Syria and Cilicia. Parthia was not even under Roman control.

questions.stem: A silver denarius from the late 30s BCE shows Antony with the legend ANTONI ARMENIA DEVICTA and Cleopatra with CLEOPATRAE REGINAE REGVM FILIORVM REGVM ('of Cleopatra, queen of kings and of her sons who are kings'). What does the coin best show?
options: Antony's Armenian campaign failed and Cleopatra was forced to pay for his losses
Antony promoted Cleopatra's royal status on a Roman coin linked to his eastern victory
Cleopatra was officially recognised by the senate as joint ruler of the Roman state
Octavian issued coins mocking Cleopatra's titles to stir up hostility against her
questions.explanation: The coin pairs Antony's claim to have conquered Armenia with titles for Cleopatra and her children that echo the Donations of Alexandria. Putting a foreign queen on a Roman denarius was striking, and it helps explain why Octavian could portray the partnership as a threat.

questions.stem: Coins struck under Cleopatra show a strong profile with a large hooked nose, very different from her image in films. The best caution about using them as evidence of her appearance is that:
options: no coins were issued with her portrait, so these must be modern forgeries
Egyptian law banned accurate images of a living queen on any coinage
royal coin portraits were political images and may not be realistic likenesses
the coins were made after her death on Octavian's orders to make her look unattractive
questions.explanation: A ruler's coin portrait was a deliberate statement of authority, often stylised to suggest strength or continuity with a dynasty. Coins with her portrait were struck in her lifetime, so they are genuine evidence of how she chose to be shown.

questions.stem: On the Temple of Hathor at Dendera, Cleopatra and Caesarion appear in traditional Egyptian style making offerings to the gods, while her coins show a Greek royal portrait. A historian would most likely conclude that Cleopatra:
options: was worshipped only by Greeks and never by Egyptians
ordered the reliefs to show her submission to Rome
used different images of her rule for different audiences
abandoned Greek culture completely after Caesar's murder in 44 BCE
questions.explanation: Temple reliefs addressed Egyptian priests and subjects in the language of pharaonic kingship, while Greek coin portraits spoke to the Hellenistic world. Together they show a ruler adapting her image to her audiences.

questions.stem: A papyrus of 33 BCE grants tax privileges to a Roman landholder and ends with one word in a different hand, 'ginesthoi' ('let it be done'). Some scholars think Cleopatra wrote it, others doubt this. The safest use of the document is as evidence that:
options: Cleopatra had stopped collecting taxes from Roman landowners
Cleopatra's government granted tax favours to influential Romans
Cleopatra personally wrote every royal decree issued in her name
Cleopatra could not read or write Greek and relied on scribes
questions.explanation: Whoever wrote the final word, the ordinance itself shows the crown granting privileges to a Roman, a way of winning influential support. Whether the subscription is her handwriting is debated, so claims resting on that need caution.

questions.stem: Plutarch reports that before the war of 32-31 BCE Octavian claimed Antony 'had been drugged and was not even master of himself'. This claim served Octavian by:
options: proving that Antony had already died and Cleopatra ruled in his name
persuading Cleopatra to hand Antony over to the Roman senate for trial
showing that Antony's own soldiers had begun to mutiny against him
presenting the war as one against Cleopatra rather than a civil war
questions.explanation: War was declared on Cleopatra alone, and portraying Antony as bewitched let Octavian avoid attacking a fellow Roman directly. The claim is propaganda reported by Plutarch, not evidence of Antony's real state of mind.

questions.stem: Octavian's fleet at the Battle of Actium on 2 September 31 BCE was commanded by:
options: Gaius Cassius
Lucius Pinarius
Publius Canidius
Marcus Agrippa
questions.explanation: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, Octavian's closest general, led his fleet to victory at Actium. Canidius commanded Antony's land forces, and Cassius had died at Philippi in 42 BCE.

questions.stem: Plutarch says 'the sixty ships of Cleopatra were seen hoisting their sails for flight' at Actium and that Antony followed her. Some modern historians argue the break-out was planned. Which detail best supports their view?
options: Agrippa's fleet allowed Cleopatra's squadron to pass because she had bribed him
Cleopatra had already surrendered Alexandria to Octavian before the battle
Antony's land army joined Octavian on the morning of the battle
Antony's ships had their sails aboard, which were normally left ashore before battle
questions.explanation: Ancient warships usually left their sails on land before a sea battle, so carrying them suggests an escape was intended. Plutarch frames the flight as Antony abandoning his men out of passion, which reflects his moral purpose as much as the facts.

questions.stem: Cleopatra died in Alexandria in August 30 BCE. Which event came immediately before her death?
options: Octavian captured Alexandria and Antony took his own life
Antony was killed in battle at Actium only a few days earlier
Caesarion was crowned king of Egypt by Octavian's army
The Roman senate offered her an alliance on equal terms
questions.explanation: After Actium, Octavian invaded Egypt in 30 BCE. Antony died by suicide as Alexandria fell, and Cleopatra died soon after, while in Octavian's custody.

questions.stem: Plutarch tells the story of the asp but adds 'the truth of the matter no one knows'. Cassius Dio says the only marks on her body were slight pricks on the arm and mentions a poisoned hairpin. What can a historian most safely conclude?
options: She died of illness, and the suicide story is invented
Cleopatra took her own life, but how she did it is uncertain
Octavian's soldiers killed her and spread the snake story
The asp story is proven because both writers mention it
questions.explanation: The sources agree she chose death but admit they do not know the method, offering several versions. Mentioning the asp is not proof of it, since both writers present it as one report among others.

questions.stem: Horace's ode on Cleopatra's death says she would not be led as a private woman in a proud triumph. In Octavian's triumph of 29 BCE, Plutarch reports:
options: Cleopatra's body was carried in an open coffin through the streets of Rome
Caesarion walked in chains behind Octavian's chariot
Antony's statue was smashed by the crowd in the Forum
an image of Cleopatra with the asp clinging to her was carried
questions.explanation: By dying, Cleopatra avoided being paraded as Arsinoe had been in Caesar's triumph, so Octavian displayed an effigy instead. This shows that avoiding public humiliation in Rome was a likely motive for her suicide.

questions.stem: Which was a direct consequence of Cleopatra's death in 30 BCE?
options: Caesarion ruled Egypt as a client king under Roman supervision
Cleopatra Selene was crowned queen of Egypt by the Roman senate
Egypt became a Roman province governed by a prefect appointed by Octavian
Egypt was shared out between Herod of Judaea and the kings of Parthia
questions.explanation: Octavian annexed Egypt and placed it under an equestrian prefect answerable to him, ending the Ptolemaic dynasty. Caesarion was put to death on Octavian's orders, removing a rival 'son of Caesar'.

questions.stem: In Odes 1.37 Horace calls the queen 'fatale monstrum' (a deadly monster) without naming her, yet ends by praising her courage in choosing death. This mixture is best explained by the fact that Horace:
options: secretly supported Antony and hid his true views in his poetry for safety
was an Egyptian poet writing for Cleopatra's own court
wrote long after Augustus died, when views had softened
celebrated Octavian's victory, which a worthy enemy made greater
questions.explanation: Horace was a poet in Maecenas's circle writing soon after Actium, so his ode celebrates Octavian. Granting Cleopatra a proud death makes Octavian's enemy, and so his victory, more impressive.

questions.stem: Horace's ode describes Caesar chasing the queen as she flees 'from Italy' and says hardly a single ship of hers escaped the flames. For a historian reconstructing Actium, the ode is best used as:
options: the official record of the battle, copied from Octavian's own dispatches
proof that Cleopatra's whole fleet was destroyed before it could escape
evidence of how the victory was celebrated in Rome, not a reliable narrative
an eyewitness account of the battle, since Horace served on Agrippa's ship
questions.explanation: Cleopatra fled from Actium in Greece, not Italy, and her squadron escaped, so the poem compresses and exaggerates events. Its value lies in showing the triumphant Roman view of the queen.

questions.stem: Cassius Dio writes that Cleopatra 'was of insatiable passion and insatiable avarice' and 'captivated the two greatest Romans of her day'. In evaluating this judgment, it matters most that Dio:
options: relied only on Egyptian temple records that were favourable to the queen
wrote while Cleopatra was alive and therefore feared her punishment
was a Roman senator writing over two centuries later in a hostile tradition
was a member of Cleopatra's own court who had a personal grudge against the queen
questions.explanation: Dio wrote his Roman History in Greek in the early third century CE, drawing on a tradition shaped by Octavian's victory. His summary is a moral verdict, not a neutral assessment of her rule.

questions.stem: Plutarch writes that Cleopatra's beauty 'was in itself not altogether incomparable' and that her charm lay in her conversation. How does this affect a common later image of her?
options: It confirms she spoke only Greek and no other languages
It weakens the idea that she won power through beauty alone
It proves Roman writers thought she was unattractive and dull
It shows Plutarch had seen her portrait statues in Alexandria
questions.explanation: Plutarch stresses her intelligence, voice and conversation rather than looks, which cuts against the stereotype of a seductress relying on beauty. He also reports that she spoke many languages.

questions.stem: Plutarch says the physician Philotas told Plutarch's grandfather Lamprias about Antony's life in Alexandria, and he names Olympus, Cleopatra's physician, as a source for her last days. These details mean Plutarch's Life of Antony:
options: relied only on Octavian's memoirs and so has no other evidence
preserves some material from eyewitnesses, passed on second-hand
is a contemporary diary written by people at Cleopatra's court
can be fully trusted because doctors had no reason to be biased
questions.explanation: Plutarch wrote more than a century after her death, but these named informants suggest some details came from people close to events. The material was still second-hand, oral and selected to suit Plutarch's moral portrait of Antony.

questions.stem: Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra (first performed in the early 1600s) drew mainly on:
options: Cleopatra's own letters, published in London
the Res Gestae of Augustus, found in Ankara
Egyptian temple inscriptions, read in Greek
Plutarch's Life of Antony, in English translation
questions.explanation: Shakespeare followed Thomas North's English translation of Plutarch's Lives closely, so the play passes on Plutarch's picture of a passionate Antony undone by Cleopatra. The Egyptian scripts were not deciphered until the nineteenth century.

questions.stem: Films such as Cleopatra (1963), starring Elizabeth Taylor, show a glamorous queen in lavish costumes. A historian evaluating this representation would most likely argue that it:
options: is based mainly on Egyptian sources written by Cleopatra's supporters
proves that Plutarch's account of her appearance was mistaken
reflects its own era's ideas of glamour more than the ancient evidence
is the most accurate source because it used every surviving papyrus
questions.explanation: Each period remakes Cleopatra to suit its own tastes and anxieties, from Augustan propaganda to Hollywood spectacle. Films draw on the Roman literary tradition and add invention, so they are evidence of later attitudes rather than of her life.

questions.stem: Many modern historians portray Cleopatra as a capable ruler and strategist rather than a seductress. The main reason for this change in interpretation is:
options: the finding of her tomb, which contained her official state records
greater awareness that the literary sources come from her enemies' side
the discovery of her full autobiography in the library of Alexandria
new evidence that she won the Battle of Actium and was later betrayed
questions.explanation: Historians now read Plutarch, Dio and the Augustan poets as shaped by Octavian's victory, and weigh them against coins, papyri and inscriptions. Her tomb has never been found, and no writings of her own survive beyond, possibly, one word.

questions.stem: Which judgment best assesses Cleopatra's significance in her own time?
options: Her victory at Actium allowed the Ptolemaic dynasty to keep Egypt until the reign of Hadrian
Her alliance with the Parthians forced Rome to abandon all its provinces in the eastern Mediterranean
Her alliance with Antony shaped the last civil war of the Republic, whose outcome made Octavian sole ruler
Her rule ended Roman involvement in Egypt, which stayed independent for the next three centuries
questions.explanation: Cleopatra's resources and partnership with Antony made Egypt central to the struggle between Antony and Octavian, and her defeat left Octavian master of the Roman world and of Egypt's wealth. Egypt became a Roman province on her death.
